_comment: Source for scripts/solve_games.py. Payoffs are ordinal, chosen so each game has its canonical structure. Equilibria are computed, never typed here.

games.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
games.life: Trust with someone you may not deal with again
games.reading: Defecting beats cooperating whatever the other does, so both defect and both end on 1 when they could have had 3.
games.move: Make the relationship repeat. When the future matters enough, conditional cooperation becomes rational.

games.name: Stag Hunt
games.life: Cofounders, marriage, any ambitious joint bet
games.reading: Hunting stag pays more when both commit. Hare pays less but remains safe when the other person wavers. Doubt drives this game.
games.move: Buy assurance before you commit. Evidence that they will show up is worth more than a better offer.

games.name: Chicken
games.life: Ego standoffs, brinkmanship, who blinks first
games.reading: Two equilibria, and in each one somebody swerves. The crash is worst for both, which is exactly why the threat works.
games.move: Build a face-saving exit for them. Cornering someone in Chicken raises your odds of the crash.

games.name: Trust Game
games.reading: Sending creates value only if it comes back. Backward induction says they keep, so you never send, and the surplus is never made.
games.move: Send a small amount first. Escalate on evidence, not on how trustworthy they sound.

games.name: Public Goods
games.life: Housework, team effort, anything everyone benefits from
games.reading: Everyone wants the shared good and would prefer someone else to fund it. Free-riding dominates, so the good stays underfunded.
games.move: Make each contribution visible. People often free-ride on work they cannot see.

games.name: Coordination
games.life: Two good options, and being together beats being right
games.reading: You each prefer a different option, but a mismatch pays nobody. Both matching outcomes are stable.
games.move: Agree a focal point in advance, or alternate. Arguing over which is better wastes the surplus you are arguing about.

games.name: Matching Pennies
games.life: Genuinely adversarial: bluffing, bidding, tactical surprise
games.reading: No pure equilibrium exists. Any pattern you settle into can be exploited, so stable play requires unpredictability.
games.move: Reserve zero-sum tactics for genuinely adversarial games. Applied elsewhere, they burn value both sides could have kept.

games.name: Principal-Agent
games.life: Managing, delegating, hiring anyone whose effort you cannot see
games.reading: Monitoring is costly and can damage trust. Without it, hidden effort invites shirking. The problem begins with poor visibility.
games.move: Make the outcome observable and reward it directly. Better evidence reduces the need to police behaviour.

levers.ask: Who is at the table, and who could be?
levers.example: A bad cofounder is rarely a negotiation problem. It is a casting problem.

levers.ask: What is each person rewarded for?
levers.example: If comp rewards beating colleagues, no amount of asking for collaboration will produce it.

levers.ask: Who knows what, and what stays hidden?
levers.example: Mistrust often means low observability. Make the work visible before appealing to good faith.

levers.ask: Who moves first, and can that change?
levers.example: Split one irreversible commitment into stages and each stage buys information for the next.

levers.ask: Which constraints are real, and which are just habit?
levers.example: Constant interruption is a protocol failure. Set the protocol rather than absorbing the cost.

levers.ask: Is this the right place to be playing at all?
levers.example: In a commodity market everyone competes on price. Differentiate, or find a market where you are scarce.

levers.ask: What happens if you walk, and how good is that?
levers.example: Your bargaining power is set before the negotiation by how survivable no-deal is.

laws.why: Nothing compounds after ruin. Expected value stops being the right measure once a loss ends your ability to keep playing.
The same people come back. That is what makes reputation an asset and betrayal expensive.
Treating a joint problem as a contest destroys the surplus you were both there to create.
One promotion, one contract, one auction. Misreading these as cooperative is its own kind of loss.
Evaluate a decision after everyone else has replied to it.

laws.law: Change the game before playing harder
laws.why: Effort inside a badly structured game is the most expensive way to lose.
Under uncertainty, a cheap experiment is usually worth more than a confident decision.
Small bet, then evidence, then large bet. Reversing that order is how people lose big.
What you already spent is a fact about the past. Only future costs and benefits are decidable.
Bargaining power is built before the conversation, by making no-deal survivable.
It takes years to build and one transaction to spend. Price it accordingly.
When the stated goal and the reward structure disagree, the reward structure wins.

laws.law: Avoid success that costs you agency
laws.why: A well-paid role you cannot leave is a trap that looks like an achievement.
Ask whether today's choice improves the sequence of states that follows.
Strong players spend less of their life in games where winning means nothing.

dashboard.ask: Is capability compounding, or just responsibility?
Do I capture upside from the value I create?
Does home restore energy or consume it?
Am I deciding from equilibrium or from strain?
Am I gaining useful future options?
Are more of these relationships built on trust?
Are my claims backed by evidence?
Does my authority match my responsibility?
Would I value this life with no spectators?
Do I have more credible moves than a year ago?

classifier.q: Who are the players, including future you?
classifier.why: Present you and future you have different incentives and rarely negotiate.
Compare what they say with the choices they repeatedly make.
Order determines who commits and who responds, and often decides the outcome.
One-shot and repeated versions of the same game have opposite correct strategies.
Zero-sum tactics can destroy value when both sides could have gained.
Hidden information is where most bad deals are made.

classifier.q: What happens if I refuse to play?
classifier.why: Your no-deal outcome sets your bargaining power before you say anything.
Reversible decisions reward speed. Irreversible ones reward patience.
The move that fails is usually the one that assumed nobody would react.
